open_questions: High-contrast imaging or RV could test the massive companion implied by secondary and phase curve, but TESS alone already favours EB.
dossier.public_summary: The light curve shows a second eclipse almost as deep as the first at a different phase and large out-of-eclipse variations, plus huge sector-to-sector depth changes including a non-detection and an outlier five times deeper. Combined with extreme starspot variability at half the signal period, this is best explained as a blended or nearby eclipsing binary rather than a 1.9-Earth-radius planet.

reasons.why: Second dip at 0.6188 phase is strong (well above best_brightening_snr 3.939) and ~57% of the primary depth: phase offset 0.1188 from 0.5 and depth ratio are inconsistent with a planetary occultation and favour a stellar companion eclipse.

Large out-of-transit swing at this period with a very large-amplitude spot modulation at ~7.4 d exactly half the 14.4-d signal period points to ellipsoidal/phase variations from a close binary and spot modulation rather than a planet.
reasons.value: phase_curve amplitude_ppm 103 ratio_to_depth 0.2185 chi2 56.86 dof 9; rotation amplitude_ppm 50455-61146 signal_over_rotation 1.9419707290753356

reasons.why: Depth truly changes between TESS-SPOC sectors (including a negative depth in S64 and double depth in S65) and is source-dependent, inconsistent with a steady planetary transit.

Individual transits do not agree in depth, a classic blend/binary signature, with the signal driven by a few anomalous events and apparent depth far above a 1.924 Rearth, 1.749 h flat-bottomed flat signature.
